## In Praise of the Unnoticed

The path through the park was the same path I had taken a hundred times, which is precisely why I did not see it. My feet knew the way, my eyes were elsewhere—on the small illuminated rectangle in my palm, where the day’s grievances and amusements flowed past like a river of glass beads. I was engaged in that most modern of occupations: absorbing information while experiencing nothing. The sun was setting, or rising, I could not have said which; the light was merely a condition, not a presence. And then, because the sidewalk buckled at one familiar spot, I stumbled, and in the moment of looking down to recover my balance, I saw it: a single dandelion, not in a bed or a border, but thrusting through a crack in the concrete, its head a perfect geometry of yellow florets. I stopped. I put the phone away. I knelt, with the unselfconsciousness of a child—or a fool—and looked.

That dandelion did something to me. It was not a revelation; it was not beautiful in any transcendent sense. It was simply there, entire, alive, indifferent to my dramas. And I realized, with a small shock, that I had not truly looked at a plant in weeks. I had seen lawns, trees, flowerbeds—they registered as background furniture. But I had not *encountered* a living thing. I had not allowed a leaf to fill my whole field of vision, to trace its veins, to wonder at the cellular ferocity that pushed it through asphalt. In that moment the dandelion was not a weed; it was a lesson. It said, as plainly as anything can say: you are missing the world.

This is not an original confession. It is the confession of an age. We live, as every commentator reminds us, in an economy of attention, where our minds are the raw material extracted by algorithms and monetized by advertisers. The metaphors we use are industrial: we talk of *scrolling*, *streaming*, *surfing*—all movement, all flow, all restless locomotion across surfaces. What we rarely talk about is stillness. What we rarely talk about is the act of stopping. Attention has become a scarce resource, not because we are incapable of concentrating, but because we have trained ourselves out of the habit. We have outsourced our curiosity to recommendation engines. We have let the world be mediated, curated, and delivered to us in packets, each one designed to be slightly more gripping than the last. And the price of this convenience is the erasure of the incidental, the overlooked, the slow—all the small wonders that make a life feel inhabited rather than merely operated.

I used to know this. As a child, I did not need to be taught to pay attention; I had not yet learned to be distracted. I remember a creek behind my grandmother’s house, a narrow ribbon of brown water that any adult would have dismissed as drainage. But to me it was an ocean. I would lie on my stomach on the bank for what felt like hours, watching water striders skate across the surface tension, their feet dimpling the film without breaking it. I would scoop up handfuls of mud and sift for worms, for the translucent eggs of snails, for the tiny armored triops that would appear, like visitors from another epoch, in the warm shallows. The world was not backdrop; it was a dense, buzzing, infinite text, and I was learning to read it with my whole body. I felt time not as a line but as a pool, deep and still. An afternoon could contain a thousand years.

What happened to that child? The usual things. School happened, with its bells and schedules, its insistence on one subject at a time and its implicit lesson that knowledge is something you acquire at a desk, not something you encounter in a creek. Puberty happened, bringing the terrible self-consciousness that turns every glance outward into a mirror. Technology happened, first television, then the internet, then the smartphone, each one more adept than the last at filling the empty spaces where noticing used to grow. And slowly, incrementally, I replaced the world with representations of the world. I did not stop seeing; I stopped *looking*. The difference is not semantic. To see is to register light on the retina. To look is to bring the full weight of one’s attention to bear on something, to ask it questions, to wait for answers. Looking is a kind of conversation. Seeing is just a transaction.

The dandelion stopped me, but it did not save me. That would be too neat. What it did was remind me that I had a choice. Attention, I have come to believe, is not a fixed capacity but a muscle, and like any muscle it can be strengthened, or it can atrophy. The act of noticing is a discipline, one of the oldest in the world, though we tend to hide it under other names. The artist’s discipline, the scientist’s discipline, the mystic’s discipline—all are, at bottom, the same practice: sustained, open, patient attention to what is present. The haiku poet who writes about a frog jumping into an old pond is not being whimsical; she is doing the most serious work there is, the work of registering the exact texture of an instant. The naturalist who sits motionless for an hour to watch a bird build its nest is not wasting time; he is participating in the vast, slow conversation of life. The contemplative who repeats a single word for decades is not trying to empty the mind, but to fill it—with the ordinary, the immediate, the sacred-in-the-common.

The great teachers of attention are often the most surprising. Consider the Japanese artist and essayist Tanizaki, who wrote a whole book in praise of shadows, arguing that beauty is not something you add to a room but something you reveal by allowing darkness to remain. He was not talking about interior design; he was talking about a mode of perception. To notice shadows is to notice the spaces between things, the quiet places that modern life is always trying to eliminate with more light, more noise, more signal. Or consider the naturalist Bernd Heinrich, who spent years studying ravens and discovered that they imitate predators and play with objects—not because they are foraging, but because they are curious. Curiosity, in Heinrich’s ravens, is not a means to an end; it is an end in itself. That is what attention looks like when it is not enslaved to utility. It is a form of play.

I began, after the dandelion, to experiment. I would take walks without my phone, and instead of listening to a podcast or a playlist, I would listen to the place itself—the wind in the sycamores, the scolding of a jay, the distant hum of a lawnmower, the way my own breathing changed as I climbed a hill. At first this was excruciating. The absence of stimulation felt like withdrawal, and in a sense it was. My brain, conditioned to novelty, kept reaching for a pocket that was vacant. But after a week or two, something shifted. The sounds began to separate, to acquire texture and location. I could hear the difference between a finch and a sparrow, not because I had learned their calls from an app, but because I had sat still long enough to notice that one song rises while the other falls. I began to see the same differentiation in the visual field. The park, which had been a green blur, resolved into distinct biographies: the oak with a scar where lightning had split its trunk, the patch of plantain that grew where field mice had disturbed the soil, the dead branch where a pileated woodpecker had hammered into a carpenter-ant nest, leaving chips of wood like blond sawdust on the ground. None of this was useful. All of it was necessary.

The writer and farmer Wendell Berry has a phrase: “the peace of wild things.” He wrote a short poem of that title, in which he lies down in the grass and lets the wild things—the wood drake, the great heron—restore his soul. But what strikes me about that poem is that Berry does not merely lie down. He *watches*. The wood drake is not an emblem; it is a bird. The heron is not a symbol; it is a bird, feeding in the shallows. The poem works because Berry’s attention is specific. He does not say “I saw some birds and felt calm.” He says, “I come into the peace of wild things who do not tax their lives with forethought of grief.” The wild things are at peace precisely because they are not elsewhere. They are entirely where they are. To watch them is to be invited, for a moment, into that same state.

This is the discipline of noticing, and it has a moral dimension that we often overlook. Attention is the beginning of care. You cannot love what you do not see. You cannot protect what you have not noticed is endangered. The environmental movement, at its best, has understood this. The reason we protect a wetland is not because of an abstract argument about ecosystem services; it is because someone took the time to wade into it, to see the heron, to hear the chorus of frogs, to be changed by the encounter. The great nature writers—Aldo Leopold, Rachel Carson, Terry Tempest Williams—all make the same move: they render the particular with such vividness that the reader feels complicit in its fate. Leopold’s “thinking like a mountain” begins with a mountain on which he has shot a wolf, and the dying fire in the wolf’s eyes. The essay is a confession of inattention, a testimony to the moment he saw the consequences of not noticing.

And yet, if I am honest, my own rediscovery of attention has not been consistently noble. It has been a struggle, full of lapses. I still catch myself reaching for my phone at red lights. I still drift through conversations, composing responses while the other person is speaking. I still walk through a beautiful landscape with my mind two hours ahead, rehearsing a meeting or replaying an argument. The muscle atrophies quickly; it takes only a few days of neglect to lose the tone I had gained. But the good news is that it strengthens quickly too. A single morning of sitting in the garden, watching the bees work the lavender, is enough to recalibrate my sense of time. The bees do not know the concept of a deadline. They move from flower to flower with a kind of lavish inefficiency, each visit an end in itself. Watching them, I remember that attention is not a resource to be hoarded but a joy to be indulged.

I have found that the practice of noticing spills over into other areas of life, including the most human one: the act of listening. To truly listen to another person is a form of attention that is vanishingly rare. Most of us do not listen; we wait. We wait for the other to finish so that we can speak, or we wait for the pause into which we can insert our advice or our anecdote. But what would it mean to listen without agenda, without the need to reply? What would it mean to hear the other person’s words as if they were the first words ever spoken, as if the speaker were a stranger from a distant country? This is, strangely enough, a spiritual practice. The theologian Paul Tillich said that the first duty of love is to listen. Not to fix, not to solve, not to teach—just to listen. That kind of listening creates space. It says: you are here. Your experience matters. I am willing to be changed by your account of the world.

I tried this once, deliberately, with an elderly neighbor. She was a woman I had avoided for years because she talked slowly and at length about her garden, her children, her ailments. I had categorized her as boring, which is to say, I had not actually heard a word she had said. One afternoon I decided to practice attention. I sat on her porch and listened for an hour. She told me about the peonies her mother had planted in 1948, how she had dug them up and moved them three times, how they always bloomed on her birthday regardless of the weather. She told me about her husband, dead twenty years, who had been a lineman for the electric company, how he had fallen off a pole in a storm and broken his back, how he had never complained and had built her a greenhouse with his own hands while still in a body cast. She told me about the mockingbird that had learned to imitate the sound of the school bus’s air brakes, and how it had fooled her every morning for a month. When I left, I felt as if I had traveled to another country. None of this information was useful. All of it was vital. She was not boring; I was bored, which is its own kind of blindness.

There is a word in Japanese, *yūgen*, that is often translated as “profound, mysterious beauty,” but which really refers to the sense of deep meaning that lies beneath the surface of ordinary things. To perceive *yūgen* is to feel, in the presence of a sunset or a single autumn leaf on a stone, the vastness of time, the fragility of existence, the interweaving of all life. It is not something you can grasp; it is something that grasps you. But I believe it is more available than we think. It does not require a trip to a remote mountain or a cathedral. It requires only the willingness to stop, to look, to listen. To notice the way light falls on a kitchen table at 4 p.m. To notice the crumbs of yesterday’s bread still in the grain of the wood. To notice the sound of your own breathing, which you have carried with you every moment of your life and almost never heard.

The essayist Rebecca Solnit begins her book *A Field Guide to Getting Lost* with a meditation on the word “lost.” She writes that “lost” once meant not only being unable to find your way but also being “occult, or hidden, or secret.” To be lost is to be caught in a state of not-knowing, which can be terrifying, but which is also the condition of discovery. I wonder if our age is lost in the more obvious sense—overwhelmed, anxious, unable to find a path through the noise. And I wonder if the remedy is not more navigation but more attention. To be present is, paradoxically, to be found. When I am sitting on the damp ground looking at a dandelion, I know exactly where I am: in a body, on a planet, at one moment in a chain of moments that stretches back to the first cell and forward to whatever will come after. That knowledge does not solve anything. It is not a plan or an answer. But it is a ground. It is a place to stand.

The dandelion has gone, of course. It was mowed down the next week by the city crew, who saw it as a weed and not as a messenger. But its offspring are scattered across the park, and each spring brings a new generation. I pass the old crack in the sidewalk on my walks, and sometimes I stop to see what has moved in: a tuft of crabgrass, a prostrate knotweed, a small and nameless moss. The crack is a memorial to my rediscovery of the obvious: that the world is always offering itself to us, in infinite detail, and that we are the ones who turn away. We are the ones who choose the screen over the sky, the algorithm over the avenue, the feed over the field. It does not have to be that way. We can choose to look. We can choose to listen. We can choose, one small act of attention at a time, to return to the living world.

On my darker days, I wonder if this is enough. There is so much suffering, so much injustice, so much deliberate cruelty being done to the earth and to one another. What good is watching a bee? What difference does one person’s noticing make against the roar of the machinery? And then I remember that every movement for justice, every act of compassion, every repair of a broken thing began with someone noticing. Someone looked at a polluted river and said, “This is not right.” Someone looked at an overcrowded classroom, an unsafe workplace, a dying patient, a wounded soldier, and refused to look away. Attention is the first act of love and the first act of politics. To notice is to be implicated. Once you have truly seen a thing, you cannot pretend it does not exist. The moral life begins not with principles but with perception.

So I write this as a kind of letter to myself, a reminder that the world is still here. The sun is still setting, not on a screen but in the sky, where it does every evening with a lightshow that no algorithm can capture. The heron is still standing in the shallows, patient as a lesson. The ants are still moving their eggs along the cracked sidewalk, ceaseless as thought. The voice of my neighbor is still speaking, if I will only sit and listen. None of these things will make the news. None of them will trend. But they are, in a much truer sense, the news: the ongoing, unspeakable, miraculous fact of existence. To attend to them is to practice a form of resistance—not against anything, but for everything. For the leaf. For the bird. For the other person who is, right now, trying to tell you something. For the life that is not somewhere else but here, not someday but now, not in the feed but in the flesh. We can walk out of the house with our eyes open. We can let the dandelion stop us. We can stay, for as long as it takes, to be present to what is present. That is all. That is everything.
